gap: No result ChatGPT got converts the warranty floors into kWh still guaranteed at the end of the warranty: a FranklinWH aPower 2 is guaranteed 10.5 kWh at year 15 (70% of 15 kWh) and an Enphase IQ Battery 10C only 6.0 kWh at year 15 (60% of 10 kWh), even though both cards say "15-year warranty", while a Powerwall 3 is guaranteed 9.45 kWh at year 10.
standout_why: I compared against four pages. EnergySage's whole-home page (cited, 2026-05-11) gives "10 years at 70%" for Powerwall 3 and "15 years at 70%" for aPower 2, but it does not cover Enphase at all, so it never shows the 60% floor. Solar.com (cited, 2026-10-01) gives warranty years only and says generally that warranties keep "about 70%". SolarExaminer's comparison (cited, 2026-10-24) lists "15 years, 60 MWh" and "15 years, 6,000 cycles" without any retention percentage. Home Battery Report's warranty table was in one chat's results but not cited. It does list the per-model percentages (Enphase 10C: 70% at year 10, 60% at end of term), but it never converts them into guaranteed kWh or into full-cycle equivalents. So the percentages are already in that uncited result, and the kWh comparison is new.
decides: ChatGPT's cards put "15-year warranty" on both FranklinWH aPower 2 and Enphase IQ Battery 10C as if the two were equal. Once you normalise them, Franklin's 15 years guarantees 1.75× the end-of-term energy (10.5 kWh vs 6.0 kWh). Powerwall 3's shorter 10-year warranty still guarantees more energy at year 10 than the 10C does (9.45 kWh vs 7.0 kWh). This backs ChatGPT's pick of Powerwall 3 and aPower 2 over the 10C. It also weakens the 10C's "15-year warranty" selling point unless the shopper is tied to Enphase microinverters.

findings.label: Warranty floor, normalised
findings.value: 70% of 13.5 kWh at 10 years = 9.45 kWh guaranteed; unlimited cycles for solar self-consumption, time-based control and backup; 37.8 MWh throughput cap for other uses
findings.source_title: Home battery warranty comparison: all 17 models in one table | The Home Battery Report
findings.note: Named reviewer is the third-tier source. tesla.com/powerwall returned 403, and the US warranty PDF on digitalassets.tesla.com is AES-encrypted, so the tools couldn't read it. Arithmetic: 13.5 × 0.70 = 9.45 kWh.

findings.label: Retention as cited rival states it
findings.source_title: What are the best batteries for whole-home backup in 2026? | EnergySage
findings.note: Page updated 2026-05-11. This independently confirms the 70% figure.

findings.label: Warranty term and throughput (maker)
findings.value: 15 years / 60 MWh throughput; 10 kW continuous; surge to start a 5-ton A/C
findings.note: The maker page says "extended 15-year warranty for 60 MWh throughput" but gives no retention percentage. Normalised: 60 MWh ÷ 15 kWh = 4,000 full-cycle equivalents before the warranty can end early.

findings.label: Warranty floor, normalised
findings.value: 70% of 15 kWh rated = 10.5 kWh guaranteed at end of 15 years or 60 MWh, whichever comes first
findings.source_title: Home battery warranty comparison: all 17 models in one table | The Home Battery Report
findings.note: The 70% comes from the reviewer's table, which quotes the Franklin warranty ("not less than 70% of the rated capacity"). EnergySage, read the same day, also lists "15 years at 70%". Arithmetic: 15 × 0.70 = 10.5 kWh.

findings.label: Capacity, power and warranty term (maker)
findings.value: 10 kWh usable; 7.08 kW continuous; 15-year warranty up to 6,000 cycles
findings.note: The store page gives no retention percentage. 6,000 cycles × 10 kWh ≈ 60 MWh nominal, about the same throughput as Franklin, but the end-of-term floor is lower (next row).

findings.label: Warranty floor, normalised
findings.value: 70% of nameplate at end of year 10 = 7.0 kWh; 60% at end of term (15 years or 6,000 cycles) = 6.0 kWh
findings.source_title: Home battery warranty comparison: all 17 models in one table | The Home Battery Report
findings.note: Reviewer's row: "70 percent at the end of year 10 and 60 percent at the end of the term". Arithmetic: 10 × 0.70 = 7.0; 10 × 0.60 = 6.0 kWh. Compared with aPower 2 at year 15: 10.5 / 6.0 = 1.75×. Compared with Powerwall 3 at year 10: 9.45 vs 7.0 kWh.

findings.label: Warranty floor, normalised
findings.value: At least 60% of 5 kWh nameplate = 3.0 kWh guaranteed at end of 15 years or 6,000 cycles
findings.source_title: Home battery warranty comparison: all 17 models in one table | The Home Battery Report
findings.note: Arithmetic: 5 × 0.60 = 3.0 kWh. One chat put the 5P on a card with "15-year warranty".

findings.label: Surge figures stated on different bases
findings.value: Powerwall 3: 185 LRA motor start; aPower 2: 15 kW for 10 s; IQ Battery 5P: 7.68 kW for 3 s
findings.source_title: Best Solar Batteries of 2026: Top Picks & Real Prices | Solar.com
findings.note: This cited rival already prints these figures. The makers quote surge in different units and durations (LRA vs kW over 10 s vs kW over 3 s), so they can't be compared directly. Listed only as context, not as the gap.
